units.title: Counting the Pennies
units.caption: A furnished flat. The day before Christmas.
stanzas:
One dollar and eighty-seven cents.
That was all.
And sixty cents of it was in pennies.
Pennies saved one and two at a time
by {bulldozing|pushing and bullying} the grocer and the vegetable man and the butcher
until one’s cheeks burned with the silent {imputation|unspoken accusation} of {parsimony|being mean with money}
that such close dealing implied.
Three times Della counted it.
One dollar and eighty-seven cents.
And the next day would be Christmas.

There was clearly nothing to do
but flop down on the {shabby|old and worn out} little couch and {howl|cry very loudly}.
So Della did it.
Which {instigates|starts, sets going} the moral reflection
that life is made up of sobs, sniffles, and smiles,
with sniffles {predominating|being the biggest part}.
units.para: Della has saved money for months — and she has only one dollar and eighty-seven cents. Most of it is small pennies, saved by arguing over every price until the shopkeepers silently thought she was cheap. She counts it three times. Tomorrow is Christmas. So she falls on the old couch and cries.

units.title: The Eight-Dollar Flat
units.caption: A letter-box that takes no letters. A bell that will not ring.
stanzas:
While the mistress of the home is gradually {subsiding|calming down, sinking} from the first stage to the second,
take a look at the home.
A furnished flat at $8 per week.
It did not exactly {beggar|be too poor for} description,
but it certainly had that word on the lookout for the {mendicancy|begging} squad.

In the {vestibule|a small entrance hall} below was a letter-box into which no letter would go,
and an electric button from which no {mortal|human} finger could {coax|gently persuade} a ring.
Also appertaining thereunto was a card bearing the name
“Mr. James Dillingham Young.”

The “Dillingham” had been flung to the breeze
during a former period of {prosperity|good times, having money}
when its possessor was being paid $30 per week.
Now, when the income was shrunk to $20, though,
they were thinking seriously of contracting to a modest and unassuming D.
But whenever Mr. James Dillingham Young came home and reached his flat above
he was called “Jim” and greatly hugged by Mrs. James Dillingham Young,
already introduced to you as Della.
Which is all very good.
units.para: While Della cries, the narrator shows us the home: a rented flat for eight dollars a week, close to real poverty. Downstairs, a broken letter-box and a doorbell that does not work — and a proud name card: Mr. James Dillingham Young. Jim put up the long name when he earned thirty dollars a week. Now he earns twenty. But every evening, Della hugs him at the door and calls him Jim — and that, the narrator says, is all very good.

units.title: The Gray Cat and the Glass
units.caption: A window, a mirror, and a decision arriving.
stanzas:
Della finished her cry and attended to her cheeks with the powder rag.
She stood by the window and looked out dully
at a gray cat walking a gray fence in a gray backyard.
Tomorrow would be Christmas Day,
and she had only $1.87 with which to buy Jim a present.
She had been saving every penny she could for months, with this result.
Twenty dollars a week doesn’t go far.
Expenses had been greater than she had calculated.
They always are.
Only $1.87 to buy a present for Jim. Her Jim.
Many a happy hour she had spent planning for something nice for him.
Something fine and rare and {sterling|of true, solid quality}—
something just a little bit near to being worthy of the honor
of being owned by Jim.

There was a {pier glass|a tall narrow mirror} between the windows of the room.
Perhaps you have seen a pier glass in an $8 flat.
A very thin and very {agile|quick and light in movement} person may,
by observing his reflection in a rapid sequence of {longitudinal|up-and-down, lengthwise} strips,
obtain a fairly accurate conception of his looks.
Della, being slender, had mastered the art.

Suddenly she whirled from the window and stood before the glass.
Her eyes were shining {brilliantly|very brightly},
but her face had lost its color within twenty seconds.
Rapidly she pulled down her hair
and let it fall to its full length.
units.para: Della dries her eyes and looks out at a gray, dull world. She has planned for months to buy Jim something fine and rare — something good enough for him — and she has $1.87. Then, suddenly, she turns to the narrow mirror between the windows. Her eyes are shining, but her face goes pale: she has had an idea, and the idea costs something. She pulls down her hair and lets it fall.

units.title: The Two Treasures
units.caption: A gold watch, and hair like brown water.
stanzas:
Now, there were two possessions of the James Dillingham Youngs
in which they both took a mighty pride.
One was Jim’s gold watch that had been his father’s and his grandfather’s.
The other was Della’s hair.
Had the queen of Sheba lived in the flat across the {airshaft|a narrow open space between buildings},
Della would have let her hair hang out the window some day to dry
just to {depreciate|make something seem less valuable} Her Majesty’s jewels and gifts.
Had King Solomon been the {janitor|a building caretaker},
with all his treasures piled up in the basement,
Jim would have pulled out his watch every time he passed,
just to see him {pluck|pull sharply} at his beard from envy.

So now Della’s beautiful hair fell about her
rippling and shining like a {cascade|a small waterfall} of brown waters.
It reached below her knee
and made itself almost a garment for her.
And then she did it up again nervously and quickly.
Once she {faltered|paused, almost stopped} for a minute and stood still
while a tear or two splashed on the worn red carpet.
units.para: The couple owns two treasures. Jim's gold watch, passed down from his grandfather and father. And Della's hair, which falls below her knee like a waterfall of brown water. The narrator says even the richest queen and king in old stories would have envied them. Della lets her hair down, looks at it — then puts it up again, quickly. She stops once. Two tears fall on the worn carpet. She has decided.
gloss: a narrow open space between buildings

units.title: Madame Sofronie
units.caption: One flight up. Hair goods of all kinds.
stanzas:
On went her old brown jacket; on went her old brown hat.
With a whirl of skirts and with the brilliant sparkle still in her eyes,
she {fluttered|moved quickly and lightly} out the door and down the stairs to the street.

Where she stopped the sign read:
“Mme. Sofronie. Hair Goods of All Kinds.”
One flight up Della ran, and collected herself, {panting|breathing hard and fast}.
Madame, large, too white, {chilly|cold in manner}, hardly looked the “Sofronie.”

“Will you buy my hair?” asked Della.
“I buy hair,” said Madame.
“Take yer hat off and let’s have a sight at the looks of it.”
Down rippled the brown cascade.
“Twenty dollars,” said Madame, lifting the mass with a {practised|skilled from much repeating} hand.
“Give it to me quick,” said Della.
units.para: Della puts on her old brown jacket and hat and hurries into the street. She finds a shop sign: Mme. Sofronie — Hair Goods of All Kinds. The owner is large, pale, and cold. Della asks: "Will you buy my hair?" The woman looks, lifts the brown waterfall with an expert hand, and says: twenty dollars. Della does not stop to think. "Give it to me quick."

units.title: The Chain
units.caption: Two hours on rosy wings. Then, in a shop window—
stanzas:
Oh, and the next two hours tripped by on rosy wings.
Forget the {hashed|mixed-up, overused} metaphor.
She was {ransacking|searching wildly through} the stores for Jim’s present.

She found it at last.
It surely had been made for Jim and no one else.
There was no other like it in any of the stores,
and she had turned all of them inside out.
It was a platinum {fob chain|a short chain for a pocket watch} simple and {chaste|plain and pure in style} in design,
properly proclaiming its value by substance alone
and not by {meretricious|falsely attractive, showy} ornamentation—
as all good things should do.
It was even worthy of The Watch.
As soon as she saw it she knew that it must be Jim’s.
It was like him.
Quietness and value—the description applied to both.
Twenty-one dollars they took from her for it,
and she hurried home with the 87 cents.
With that chain on his watch
Jim might be properly anxious about the time in any company.
Grand as the watch was,
he sometimes looked at it on the sly
on account of the old leather strap that he used in place of a chain.
units.para: For two happy hours Della searches every store in town. At last she finds it: a platinum chain for Jim's pocket watch — simple, plain, valuable for what it is, not for show. "Quietness and value" — like Jim himself. It costs twenty-one dollars. She goes home with 87 cents. Now Jim can proudly check the time in front of anyone — until now, he sometimes looked at his grand watch secretly, because it hung on an old leather strap.
gloss: a short chain for a pocket watch

units.title: The Curls
units.caption: Curling irons, and forty minutes of repair.
stanzas:
When Della reached home
her {intoxication|great excitement, like being drunk on joy} gave way a little to {prudence|careful good sense} and reason.
She got out her curling irons and lighted the gas
and went to work repairing the {ravages|serious damage} made by generosity added to love.
Which is always a tremendous task, dear friends—
a {mammoth|huge} task.

Within forty minutes her head was covered with tiny, close-lying curls
that made her look wonderfully like a {truant|staying away from school without permission} schoolboy.
She looked at her reflection in the mirror
long, carefully, and critically.

“If Jim doesn’t kill me,” she said to herself,
“before he takes a second look at me,
he’ll say I look like a Coney Island chorus girl.
But what could I do—oh!
what could I do with a dollar and eighty-seven cents?”
units.para: At home, the excitement fades and worry arrives. Della heats her curling irons and spends forty minutes repairing what love has done. Now her head is covered in tiny curls, like a schoolboy's. She studies the mirror and tells herself: Jim will say I look like a cheap dancer. But what could I do with a dollar and eighty-seven cents?
gloss: great excitement, like being drunk on joy
staying away from school without permission

units.title: The Stare
units.caption: Seven o'clock. A step on the stair.
stanzas:
At 7 o’clock the coffee was made
and the frying-pan was on the back of the stove
hot and ready to cook the chops.

Jim was never late.
Della doubled the fob chain in her hand
and sat on the corner of the table near the door that he always entered.
Then she heard his step on the stair away down on the first flight,
and she turned white for just a moment.
She had a habit of saying a little silent prayer
about the simplest everyday things,
and now she whispered:
“Please God, make him think I am still pretty.”

The door opened and Jim stepped in and closed it.
He looked thin and very serious.
Poor fellow, he was only twenty-two—
and to be burdened with a family!
He needed a new overcoat and he was without gloves.

Jim stopped inside the door,
as {immovable|unable to be moved} as a {setter|a hunting dog that freezes when it finds a bird} at the scent of {quail|a small game bird},
His eyes were fixed upon Della,
and there was an expression in them that she could not read,
and it terrified her.
It was not anger, nor surprise, nor {disapproval|thinking something is wrong or bad}, nor horror,
nor any of the {sentiments|feelings} that she had been prepared for.
He simply stared at her fixedly
with that {peculiar|strange, unusual} expression on his face.
units.para: Seven o'clock. Coffee ready, pan hot. Della sits by the door with the chain in her hand and whispers a small prayer: "Please God, make him think I am still pretty." Jim comes in — thin, serious, only twenty-two, needing a new coat, with no gloves. And then he stops. He stares at her with an expression she cannot read. Not anger. Not surprise. Not horror. Something else — and it frightens her.
gloss: a hunting dog that freezes when it finds a bird
thinking something is wrong or bad

units.title: Sold and Gone
units.caption: “It went for you.”
stanzas:
Della wriggled off the table and went for him.
“Jim, darling,” she cried, “don’t look at me that way.
I had my hair cut off and sold
because I couldn’t have lived through Christmas
without giving you a present.
It’ll grow out again—you won’t mind, will you?
I just had to do it.
My hair grows awfully fast.
Say ‘Merry Christmas!’ Jim, and let’s be happy.
You don’t know what a nice—
what a beautiful, nice gift I’ve got for you.”

“You’ve cut off your hair?” asked Jim, {laboriously|slowly, with great effort},
as if he had not arrived at that {patent|obvious} fact yet
even after the hardest mental labor.
“Cut it off and sold it,” said Della.
“Don’t you like me just as well, anyhow?
I’m me without my hair, ain’t I?”
Jim looked about the room curiously.
“You say your hair is gone?” he said,
with an air almost of {idiocy|foolishness, not thinking clearly}.

“You needn’t look for it,” said Della.
“It’s sold, I tell you—sold and gone, too.
It’s Christmas Eve, boy. Be good to me, for it went for you.
Maybe the hairs of my head were numbered,” she went on with sudden serious sweetness,
“but nobody could ever count my love for you.
Shall I put the chops on, Jim?”

Out of his {trance|a state of staring without seeing} Jim seemed quickly to wake.
He {enfolded|wrapped his arms around} his Della.
For ten seconds let us regard with {discreet|politely careful} {scrutiny|close examination}
some inconsequential object in the other direction.
Eight dollars a week or a million a year—
what is the difference?
A mathematician or a wit would give you the wrong answer.
The magi brought valuable gifts, but that was not among them.
This dark assertion will be illuminated later on.
units.para: Della runs to him: I sold my hair — I couldn't live through Christmas without giving you a present. Jim asks again and again, slowly, as if the fact will not enter his head: "You've cut off your hair?" Della answers: sold and gone — it went for you — and no one could ever count my love. Jim wakes from his trance and holds her. The narrator looks politely away, and asks a strange question: eight dollars a week or a million a year — what is the difference? The answer, he says, will come later.
gloss: a state of staring without seeing

units.title: The Combs
units.caption: A package on the table.
stanzas:
Jim drew a package from his overcoat pocket
and threw it upon the table.
“Don’t make any mistake, Dell,” he said, “about me.
I don’t think there’s anything in the way of a haircut or a shave or a shampoo
that could make me like my girl any less.
But if you’ll unwrap that package
you may see why you had me going a while at first.”

White fingers and {nimble|quick and skilful} tore at the string and paper.
And then an {ecstatic|full of overwhelming joy} scream of joy;
and then, alas! a quick feminine change to hysterical tears and wails,
necessitating the immediate employment
of all the comforting powers of the lord of the flat.

For there lay The Combs—the set of combs, side and back,
that Della had {worshipped|loved and admired like something holy} long in a Broadway window.
Beautiful combs, pure tortoise shell, with jewelled rims—
just the shade to wear in the beautiful vanished hair.
They were expensive combs, she knew,
and her heart had simply {craved|wanted painfully} and {yearned|longed deeply} over them
without the least hope of possession.
And now, they were hers,
but the {tresses|long locks of hair} that should have adorned the {coveted|badly wanted} adornments were gone.

But she hugged them to her bosom,
and at length she was able to look up with dim eyes and a smile and say:
“My hair grows so fast, Jim!”
And then Della leaped up like a little singed cat and cried, “Oh, oh!”
units.para: Jim puts a package on the table: nothing could make me like my girl any less — but open it, and you'll see why I stared. Della tears the paper — a scream of joy — then tears. Inside are The Combs: the beautiful tortoise-shell combs she had admired in a shop window for months without any hope of owning them. Combs for hair that is gone. She hugs them, smiles through wet eyes — "My hair grows so fast, Jim!" — and then suddenly jumps up. She has remembered her own present.
gloss: loved and admired like something holy

units.title: The Watch
units.caption: An open palm. A dull precious shine.
stanzas:
Jim had not yet seen his beautiful present.
She held it out to him eagerly upon her open palm.
The dull precious metal seemed to flash
with a reflection of her bright and {ardent|burning with feeling} spirit.

“Isn’t it a dandy, Jim?
I hunted all over town to find it.
You’ll have to look at the time a hundred times a day now.
Give me your watch.
I want to see how it looks on it.”

Instead of obeying, Jim tumbled down on the couch
and put his hands under the back of his head and smiled.
“Dell,” said he, “let’s put our Christmas presents away
and keep ’em a while.
They’re too nice to use just at present.
I sold the watch to get the money to buy your combs.
And now suppose you put the chops on.”
units.para: Della holds out the chain on her open hand: "Give me your watch. I want to see how it looks on it." Jim does not reach for his watch. He lies back on the couch and smiles: let's put our presents away for a while — they're too nice to use just now. "I sold the watch to get the money to buy your combs." And then, gently: now suppose you put the chops on.

units.title: The Wisest
units.caption: The narrator turns to face you.
stanzas:
The magi, as you know, were wise men—wonderfully wise men—
who brought gifts to the Babe in the {manger|a food box for animals, used as a bed}.
They invented the art of giving Christmas presents.
Being wise, their gifts were no doubt wise ones,
possibly bearing the privilege of exchange in case of {duplication|two of the same thing}.
And here I have lamely related to you
the uneventful {chronicle|a record of events} of two foolish children in a flat
who most unwisely {sacrificed|gave up something precious} for each other
the greatest treasures of their house.
But in a last word to the wise of these days
let it be said that of all who give gifts
these two were the wisest.
Of all who give and receive gifts, such as they are wisest.
Everywhere they are wisest.
They are the magi.
units.para: The narrator ends by talking about the magi — the wise men who brought the first Christmas gifts. Their gifts were wise ones. And these two "foolish children" gave up the greatest treasures they had, for each other — hair for a watch that is sold, a chain for hair that is gone. Foolish? The narrator says the opposite: of all who give gifts, these two were the wisest. They are the magi.
gloss: a food box for animals, used as a bed
